Differences from JAX and from base R

Source: vignettes/differences.Rmd
differences.Rmd
library(jaxR)

jaxR follows JAX 0.12.0.1 closely: the same algorithms, the same dtype rules, the same random bits. This vignette lists where it differs, first for readers who know JAX, then for readers who know R, and ends with what is not ported.

For JAX users

Names

Python modules become prefixes. Transformations and core utilities keep their names.

JAX jaxR
jax.grad, jax.vmap, jax.jit grad, vmap, jit
jax.numpy.linalg.solve jnp_linalg_solve
jax.lax.while_loop lax_while_loop
jax.random.normal random_normal
jax.nn.initializers.he_normal nn_initializers_he_normal
jax.scipy.stats.norm.logpdf scipy_stats_norm_logpdf
jax.experimental.sparse.BCOO experimental_sparse_BCOO
jax.tree.map, jax.tree_util.tree_map tree_map
jax.config.update jax_config_update
jax.tree_util.Partial jax_Partial
x.at[i].set(v) at_set(x, i, v)
x.T, x.shape, x.dtype, x.astype(d) t(x), dim(x), dtype(x), jnp_astype(x, d)
x.sum(), x.reshape(s) (array methods) jnp_sum(x), jnp_reshape(x, s) (functions)

No jaxR function masks a function of base R or of the recommended packages. Where the JAX name would (jax.numpy.sum against sum), the prefixed name is exported and the base R generic gets a method: sum(x), mean(x), sin(x), x %*% y, t(x), dim(x), length(x), rev(x), rep(x, n), c(x, y) and the arithmetic, comparison and logical operators all work on jaxR arrays.

Python syntax that R does not have

Python R
x[1:3], x[::2], x[::-1] x[sl(1, 3)], x[sl(step = 2)], x[sl(step = -1)]
x[..., 0] x[ellipsis, 0]
x[None] x[newaxis]
tuples (a, b) list(a, b) or c(2L, 3L) for shapes
dicts named lists
keyword only arguments named arguments
decorators plain function calls: f <- jit(f)
context managers functions taking the code: disable_jit(code), with_jax_config(name, value, code)

Indices, axes, argnums and in_axes are 0-based, as in JAX, and negative values count from the end.

x <- jnp_arange(10)
x[0]
#> Array i32[]
#> [1] 0
x[-1]
#> Array i32[]
#> [1] 9
x[sl(2, 8, 2)]
#> Array i32[3]
#> [1] 2 4 6
jnp_sum(jnp_ones(c(2L, 3L)), axis = 0L)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 2 2 2

R values as arguments

  • An R double scalar is a weakly typed float and an R integer scalar a weakly typed integer, like Python scalars: x * 2 keeps the dtype of x.
  • A length one R vector is a scalar (rank 0), because R has no separate scalar type. Use jnp_array(5, ndmin = 1L) or jnp_reshape(v, 1L) for a vector of length one.
  • A whole valued R double is accepted where JAX wants a Python integer (shapes, axes, integer exponents in jnp_power, the arguments of jnp_arange), so x^2 uses the integer power rule and jnp_arange(5) is an integer range. The same holds for fill values: lax_full_like(x, 128) of an int8 array wraps to -128 like the Python integer 128, where the Python float 128.0 saturates to 127; R cannot tell the two apart. A fill that is not a whole number saturates as in JAX.
  • R numbers given an integer dtype convert like Python numbers in jnp.array: they are truncated toward zero, and a value outside the range of the dtype, NaN or an infinity is an error (as_jax(300, "uint8")). Conversions of arrays (jnp_astype, lax_convert_element_type) follow the device rules instead.
  • R matrices and arrays convert with their R layout: as_jax(matrix(1:6, 2)) is the 2 by 3 array you see when you print the matrix. as.array() converts back.
  • Named lists are the dictionaries of jaxR. Like JAX, pytree flattening visits the names in sorted order.
dtype(as_jax(c(1, 2), "float32") * 2)
#> [1] "float32"
dim(as_jax(3))
#> integer(0)
dtype(jnp_arange(5))
#> [1] "int32"
dtype(as_jax(1:3)^2)
#> [1] "int32"

Where jaxR accepts more than JAX

A few calls that raise in JAX are accepted in jaxR, because the R value has no exact Python counterpart. Code translated from JAX is not affected.

  • lax_* functions take R scalars of any numeric type next to an array: the scalar adopts the dtype of the array. In JAX, lax.add(x, 2.0) raises for a float32 array when 64 bit mode is on, because the Python scalar is a float64. The jnp_* functions promote like jax.numpy in both libraries.
  • lax_* functions accept negative axes (lax_rev(x, -1L), lax_concatenate(xs, -1L), lax_argmax(x, -1L, "int32")); jax.lax wants nonnegative axes.
  • An R integer vector is an int32 array in both precision modes, because R integers are 32 bit; a Python list of ints is int64 when 64 bit mode is on. An R integer scalar is a weakly typed default integer, like a Python int.
  • "float0" is accepted as a dtype name. In Python the dtype is the object jax.dtypes.float0 and the string is not understood.
  • lax_reshape() reports a wrong total size when the call is traced (jax_type_error); JAX reports it later, from the compiler (ValueError).
  • experimental_checkify_check() takes R numbers as formatting arguments; JAX wants arrays there.

Errors have the class of the Python exception (jax_type_error for TypeError, jax_value_error for ValueError, and so on, see vignette("advanced")). Messages follow JAX where the same check exists, but the wording is not guaranteed to match.

Semantics that carry over unchanged

Everything below behaves as in JAX and is listed because it differs from R:

  • Arrays are immutable. x[i] <- v works for jaxR arrays and returns a modified copy through at_set; inside jit it compiles to an in place update where that is safe.
  • The default precision is 32 bit. enable_x64() switches to 64 bit.
  • Out of bounds indices are clamped for reads and dropped for updates, there is no error.
  • Dtype promotion follows the JAX lattice, not R coercion.
  • Integer overflow wraps.
  • Functions under jit, vmap and grad must be pure and must not branch in R on array values; use jnp_where, lax_cond, lax_while_loop and friends.

Numerical agreement

Random bits and integer results agree with JAX exactly. Floating point results agree to rounding, with these known sources of last digit differences:

  • Elementary functions are evaluated by the XLA build inside the PJRT plugin. Its vectorized kernels can round differently from the build shipped in jaxlib (for example atan(Inf) in float32 is one unit in the last place below pi / 2, so a float32 Cauchy tail does not reach exactly zero).
  • On the CPU the linear algebra primitives call R’s LAPACK, which has double precision routines only: float32 factorizations (QR, SVD, eigendecompositions, LU, Cholesky) are computed in double precision and rounded, which is at least as accurate as jaxlib but not bit identical.
  • R has no 64 bit integer type. int64 and uint64 arrays compute exactly on the device, but values beyond 2^53 lose low bits when they are converted to R numbers (as.array()), and R constants beyond 2^53 cannot be written exactly.
  • The 6 bit floating point dtypes of ml_dtypes cannot be converted to R values.

Behavior that is intentionally different

  • lax_pmin and lax_pmax under vmap(..., axis_name = ) are differentiable; JAX raises an error because the rule is missing there.
  • grad(), hessian() and jacobian() forward symbolic expressions of symcompR to symcompR (see the symbolic vignette).
  • experimental_checkify_checkify() checks operations whose results are unused at the top level of the checked function, as JAX does, but not inside the bodies of lax_cond, lax_scan and lax_while_loop: jaxR removes unused code when it traces a body. Arrays in check messages are formatted by a simpler rule than NumPy’s.
  • experimental_sparse_BCOO$from_scipy_sparse() takes a sparse matrix of the Matrix package.
  • In experimental_jet_jet(), the Taylor terms of an integer constant next to a weakly typed array are weakly typed, as in JAX, when the constant meets the array in a jnp_* ufunc. Inside a function compiled with jit() the conversion of the constant has been folded away, and the terms are strongly typed; JAX keeps them weak there.
  • experimental_random_stateful_rng() without a seed draws the seed from R’s random number generator (set.seed() applies); JAX takes it from the operating system.
  • Saving and loading (jnp_save, jnp_load) read and write the NumPy .npy format, so files are interchangeable with Python.

For R users

Base R habit jaxR
1-based indices 0-based indices
x[2:4] (inclusive) x[sl(1, 4)] (end exclusive)
double precision everywhere float32 by default; enable_x64() for doubles
vectors recycle silently broadcasting follows NumPy rules; incompatible shapes are an error
column major storage printing and conversion preserve the R view of a matrix; reshaping is row major, as in NumPy
set.seed() and global random state explicit keys: random_key(), random_split()
if (x > 0) on data jnp_where() or lax_cond() inside transformed functions
for loops over elements vmap, lax_scan, lax_fori_loop
modify in place functional updates (at_set, at_add, or x[i] <- v)
NA no missing values; use NaN and the jnp_nan* reductions

Reshaping is the point that most often surprises:

m <- as_jax(matrix(1:6, 2))
m
#> Array i32[2,3]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    3    5
#> [2,]    2    4    6
jnp_reshape(m, 6L)           # row major: 1 3 5 2 4 6
#> Array i32[6]
#> [1] 1 3 5 2 4 6
as.vector(as.array(m))       # R's column major view of the same matrix
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 5 6

What is not ported

jaxR ports the single device, single process functionality of JAX. The following are outside it:

  • Multiple devices and processes: pmap across devices, jax.sharding, shard_map, jax.distributed, jax.experimental.multihost_utils. The named axis collectives (lax_psum, lax_pmean, lax_pmax, lax_pmin, lax_all_gather, …) work under vmap(..., axis_name = ).
  • Python interchange: DLPack (jax.dlpack), jax2tf, the __array__ protocols. Use .npy files (jnp_save, jnp_load) to exchange arrays with Python.
  • The profiler (jax.profiler), which drives TensorFlow’s profiler. Use monitoring_*, log_compiles() and R’s own profiler.
  • Exporting (jax.export, shape polymorphism). Compiled functions can be saved and loaded on the same platform (experimental_serialize_executable_serialize()), and the persistent compilation cache is ported (experimental_compilation_cache_set_cache_dir()).
  • Experimental modules: rnn, pallas, fused and the other small experimental modules and jax.extend. (jax.experimental.jet, jax.experimental.checkify, jax.experimental.random and jax.experimental.key_reuse are ported: experimental_jet_jet(), experimental_checkify_checkify(), experimental_random_stateful_rng() and the option jax_debug_key_reuse.)
  • XLA metadata (jax.experimental.xla_metadata): xla_metadata_call tags the operations of the function instead of staging a call operation tagged as a whole, and the operations of the backward pass are tagged only when they are staged inside the context, so ad_metadata other than "drop" is not applied.
  • The foreign function interface (jax.ffi) is ported for typed FFI handlers: ffi_register_target(), ffi_register_type(), ffi_call() and ffi_include_dir(). A handler is registered from an external pointer (getNativeSymbolInfo()) instead of a PyCapsule, so pycapsule has no counterpart. Only the execute stage of a handler can be registered, and handlers of the earlier custom call API (api_version = 0) cannot be registered, because the PJRT plugin interface does not offer either. ffi_lowering and build_ffi_lowering_function define lowering rules of new primitives, which jaxR does not expose (see jax.extend), and abstract_token results are not supported.
  • Key reuse checking records the uses of keys while a function is traced, where JAX reads its jaxpr. The rules are those of JAX, with three differences: messages name the random function (random_bits) where JAX names a jit-compiled function or says “In jit”; a traced key that passes on another (key[newaxis], traced indices) consumes all of that key when it is consumed, where JAX consumes the forwarded elements; and a function mapped by vmap() over another axis than the first consumes the whole key array.
  • Gradient accumulators (vjp_fun$with_refs(), vjp_fun$with_logs, custom_vjp_defvjp_with_accums(), custom_vjp_defvjp_with_logs() and the with_logs and with_accums arguments of custom_gradient()) compute the gradients and logs of JAX, with these differences. A rule receives the accumulator kind it declares (a ValAccum for custom_vjp_defvjp_with_accums()), where JAX gives the kind the caller asks for through with_refs() (a RefAccum for a ref, a NullAccum for ad_DontWant()) and raises a TypeError when it contradicts the declared kind. A RefAccum is a fresh ref whose value becomes an ordinary cotangent, so sparse updates are not done in place, every gradient is computed, and a ref passed to with_refs() gets its cotangent added after the backward pass. Logs of a rule inside the body of lax_scan(), lax_cond(), lax_while_loop() or checkpoint() are an error when requested (JAX stacks or sums them, or raises on a repeated key under checkpoint()); gradients are unaffected. Under vmap() logs are batched, as in JAX. custom_vjp_defremat() runs the rematerialization rule right after the forward rule, also under checkpoint(), where JAX defers it to the backward pass. A tangent of dtype float0 (of an integer value) is always a symbolic zero in jaxR, so out_nzs is FALSE for an integer output that a custom_vjp() rule marks as perturbed, where JAX reports TRUE.
  • Accelerators are not tested. The package talks to any PJRT plugin through JAXR_PJRT_PLUGIN, but the LAPACK based linear algebra is implemented for the CPU plugin only.

Python only helpers with no meaning in R (type annotations such as jax.Array and jax.typing, the abstract base classes of key paths and initializers) have no counterpart.
